checkpoints: When a proxy cache key is built from the full request URI, marketing query parameters like utm_source and utm_campaign become part of the key, so every share link to the same asset produces a distinct cache entry for identical bytes — this is cache pollution, and it prevents requests that should HIT from ever coalescing.

A Vary: Cookie header applied to every response, including public and non-personalized assets, makes the cache store one entry per session cookie instead of one shared entry per URI — an unbounded explosion that has nothing to do with the actual response bytes.

Vary: Accept-Encoding is only safe when it reflects a small canonical set of encodings (e.g. gzip, br, identity); varying on the raw, unnormalized Accept-Encoding header value fragments the cache into more entries than the number of distinct response bodies actually requires.

The fix for query-string pollution is to normalize the cache key: strip parameters that don't affect the response body (such as utm_* tracking params) and canonicalize the order of whatever parameters remain, so equivalent requests collapse onto the same entry.

Middleware that blanket-sets Vary: Cookie for session-aware responses must be scoped to only the routes whose output genuinely differs per user; it must never run in front of public, session-independent routes such as a CDN content/:key endpoint.

A falling HIT ratio paired with rising origin load points to a mismatch between the cache-key/Vary configuration and what actually changes the response, not to cache size or network/TLS problems — that mismatch is what forces otherwise-identical requests to MISS and fall through to origin.

Confirming a cache-key and Vary fix means watching the HIT ratio and the X-Cache-Status distribution climb back toward their pre-regression levels, and adding an alert on the HIT ratio so a future key or Vary regression is caught by the metric instead of discovered through an origin-load incident.

CORS is a browser-only enforcement layer checked by the client after the network response arrives, not a server-side constraint — a tool like curl that makes a raw HTTP request without a same-origin policy will show a clean 200 with correct bytes on a URL that a browser blocks entirely, because curl simply never performs the origin check that a browser does.

When a curl request against a URL succeeds while the same URL fails only in a browser, that asymmetry itself is diagnostic: it rules out the encoding pipeline, the file bytes, the status code, and the content-type as the cause, and narrows the fault to something the browser layer enforces on top of an otherwise-correct HTTP response.

The manifest handler explicitly sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` before calling `res.sendFile`, which is why the master playlist loads without issue in hls.js — the header is present exactly where it's needed for that request.

The segment handler never sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on either of its response branches — not the variant `.m3u8` playlist branch and not the `.ts` byte-serving branch — even though both branches correctly set `Content-Type` and `Cache-Control`.

A browser player using `fetch()` for segment requests is a cross-origin request whenever the player's page and the streaming service are served from different origins, a very common topology when content is fronted by a CDN; without a matching `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header, the browser blocks the response body from reaching the player's JavaScript even though the network layer received a valid HTTP 200 with the correct `video/mp2t` bytes.

The fix is to add `res.setHeader('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')` inside the segment handler for both branches (variant playlist and `.ts` segment bytes), because every HLS-serving endpoint needs the CORS header individually — setting it only on the manifest route is not sufficient for playback to continue past the first segment.

Verifying the fix requires reloading the page in an actual browser and confirming hls.js continues fetching subsequent segments with no CORS error in the console, or explicitly asserting that the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header is present on a segment response — re-running curl proves nothing, since curl never reproduced the failure in the first place and would show the same misleadingly-successful result before and after the fix.
A PURGE request that resolves without throwing only proves the HTTP call completed — it says nothing about whether the edge actually matched a stored entry and evicted it.

NGINX here keys its cache on `proxy_cache_key "$request_uri"` alone, but it still honors `Vary: Accept-Encoding` from the origin, so a single URI can back several cached variants split by content encoding.

The purge call goes out through an HTTP client shared with the service's other outbound requests, so it inherits that client's default `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br` header even though a PURGE has no business carrying it.

Sending a PURGE with an `Accept-Encoding` header makes NGINX try to match one specific encoded variant; when that doesn't line up with what's actually cached, it's a Vary mismatch and NGINX answers 412 instead of evicting anything.

A non-error HTTP status is not proof of eviction: the handler builds `{ purged: true, key }` from the fact that the outbound request resolved, without ever inspecting the status NGINX actually returned.

The origin only delegates invalidation by firing the PURGE verb — the edge is the party that decides whether an entry is actually removed, so origin-side code that assumes success is trusting a system it doesn't control.

A durable fix needs two independent pieces: stop sending `Accept-Encoding` on the PURGE call specifically (a request-scoped header override or a dedicated client instance), and set `proxy_ignore_headers Vary` on the edge so it stores exactly one entry per URI regardless of encoding.

The only trustworthy way to confirm a purge worked is to issue a fresh GET through the edge right after and check that `X-Cache-Status` flips to MISS, rather than trusting the purge handler's own optimistic response body.

Moving the fs.unlinkSync cleanup calls to the end of the try block, right after the upload succeeds, means they only run on the happy path — the moment spawnFfmpeg or uploadFromFile throws, control jumps straight to the catch, which only marks the job FAILED and never touches the temp files.

Under that refactor, every encoder or upload failure leaves both temp files — the downloaded source tmpInput and the encoder output tmpOutput — permanently orphaned on disk, since the catch path never reaches the unlink calls.

This leak compounds with volume rather than being a one-off: on a box handling any real rate of failing transcodes, accumulating orphaned temp files trends straight toward ENOSPC, at which point even healthy jobs start failing because there is no disk space left to write to.

A finally block (or a deferred cleanup registered immediately after tmpInput/tmpOutput are computed, before anything that can throw) guarantees the unlink calls execute on every exit path, success and failure alike — that guarantee is the entire reason finally exists.

outputPath is derived purely from job.inputPath, with its extension swapped for a fixed -transcoded.mp4 suffix, and carries no per-job namespace — so retrying a FAILED job against the same inputPath computes the exact same key as the earlier attempt.

Because the key is unnamespaced, a retry silently overwrites whatever the previous attempt already uploaded to MinIO; the fix is to fold the job's own id into the key (e.g. `${job.id}/${base}-transcoded.mp4`) so every attempt writes to an isolated location.

The two defects differ in blast radius and should be reported in that order: the temp-file leak can degrade the entire host over time and eventually fail every job on it, while the key collision only corrupts the single job being retried.

Confirming both fixes calls for a failure-injection test — force spawnFfmpeg or uploadFromFile to throw and assert both temp files are gone afterward, and assert that two runs against the same inputPath never produce the same outputPath.

Splitting a queue-admit operation into a separate read (`ZRANGE`) and a separate delete (`ZREM`) means the read and the removal are two independent round trips to Redis, not one atomic step — anything can happen to the sorted set in between.

When two `admit()` calls run concurrently, both can execute their `ZRANGE` against the same front-N slice before either one's `ZREM` has taken effect, so both calls observe and remove the identical set of tokens — a classic read-then-remove race condition.

That race produces a double-admit: the same shopper token gets `SADD`-ed into the admitted set by two separate calls, which means one shopper is granted entry into two concurrent checkout sessions, cascading into oversell or double-charging further down the pipeline.

Replacing the `ZRANGE` + `ZREM` pair with a single `ZPOPMIN(key, count)` call collapses the read-and-remove into one atomic Redis command — since Redis executes commands single-threaded, no two concurrent callers can ever pop the same lowest-score members.

If the admit logic needs to grow beyond a plain pop — for example checking inventory or another condition before granting a slot — that extra logic has to be wrapped in a Lua script (`EVAL`) so the whole check-and-pop sequence still executes as one atomic unit on the server, rather than reintroducing a multi-round-trip race.

The admitted-tokens `SET` is never given an `EXPIRE`, so a shopper who is admitted but then abandons the flow (closes the tab, loses connection) leaves their token sitting in that set permanently, which means effective system capacity shrinks over time even while the waiting queue still has people in it.

Fixing the capacity leak means calling `EXPIRE` on the admitted key right after the `SADD`, with the TTL sized to the real p99 checkout completion time, so abandoned grants age out and their slots recycle back to the pool automatically.

Between the two defects, the double-admit race is the higher-severity issue because it breaks correctness and can directly cause oversell or duplicate charges, while the missing TTL is a slower, gradual degradation of capacity — a fix should be validated by firing concurrent `admit()` calls and asserting the returned token arrays are strictly disjoint, plus checking that the admitted key reports a positive TTL immediately after admission.
